objectives: Explain Crew Resource Management and trace its origins from United 173 (1978) through the NASA workshop (1979) to modern CRM training requirements.
Apply James Reason's Swiss-cheese model and the SHELL model to analyze how accident chains form and break.
Describe the human factors in at least two major accidents — Tenerife (1977) and Air France 447 (2009) — and explain how automation dependency and spatial disorientation contributed.

slides.title: CRM: from United 173 to the flight deck of the A350
slides.body:
On December 28, **1978**, **United Airlines Flight 173** — a **McDonnell Douglas DC-8** with 189 people aboard — circled Portland, Oregon while the crew troubleshot an anomalous landing-gear indicator light. The captain, a highly experienced aviator, focused exclusively on the mechanical problem while the flight engineer's repeated fuel-state warnings were downplayed. The aircraft ran out of fuel and crashed in a residential area, killing 10. The **NTSB** (National Transportation Safety Board) determined that the probable cause was the captain's failure to properly monitor and respond to fuel state and the crew's failure to effectively communicate the urgency of the situation — a new category of accident cause: **crew coordination failure**.

The following year, **1979**, **NASA** convened the first **Resource Management on the Flightdeck** workshop at **Ames Research Center, Moffett Field, California**. This workshop coined the term **Crew Resource Management (CRM)** and established its core premise: cockpit accidents are most often caused not by technical incompetence but by failures in communication, leadership, situational awareness, decision-making, and workload management — the "non-technical skills." **John Lauber**, a NASA psychologist at Ames, was the primary architect of CRM as a discipline.

The **first generation of CRM** (1980s) focused on individual attitudes and leadership styles, sometimes met with pilot resistance ("charm school"). The **second generation** (late 1980s-early 1990s) developed scenario-based training with observable behavioral markers. The **third generation** (1993-present) integrated CRM into simulator training as **LOFT (Line-Oriented Flight Training)** — full-mission scenarios flown in a full-flight simulator with an observer evaluating CRM behaviors. **FAA Advisory Circular AC 120-51** (most recent edition: AC 120-51F, 2004, currently being updated) defines the training requirements. **JAR-OPS 1** (Europe, now **EASA Part-ORO**) requires CRM recurrency training annually for commercial crews.

Modern CRM frameworks address: **situational awareness (SA)** — knowing what is happening and what will happen next (Mica Endsley's three-level SA model: perception, comprehension, projection); **communication** (sterile cockpit rule below 10,000 ft, **FAR 121.542**, to eliminate distractions); **task management** and **automation management**; **decision-making** (DECIDE model, FORDEC used by **EASA**); **leadership and followership**; **threat and error management (TEM)**. The **LOSA (Line Operations Safety Audit)** program, developed by the **University of Texas Human Factors Research Project** and adopted by ICAO, uses trained observers on line flights to map threat-error-undesired aircraft state chains across an entire operation.

**Single-pilot CRM** now extends to general aviation. The **FAA WINGS** program and **AOPA Air Safety Institute** courses teach the same concepts to private pilots. The **G1000 glass cockpit**, widely installed in training aircraft (**Cessna 172SP, Piper Archer**), brought automation-management CRM challenges into the ab initio training environment for the first time.

slides.title: Tenerife, authority gradients, and the Swiss-cheese model
slides.body:
The **Tenerife airport disaster** on March 27, **1977** — a collision between a **KLM Boeing 747-206B** and a **Pan American Boeing 747-121** on the runway at **Los Rodeos Airport (TFN)** on Tenerife, Canary Islands — killed **583 people**, making it the deadliest accident in aviation history. The cause was multi-layered: a bomb at **Las Palmas (LPA)** diverted many flights to the small Tenerife airport; dense fog reduced visibility to near zero; radio frequency congestion caused simultaneous transmissions that masked a Pan Am crew's position call; and — critically — the **KLM captain, Jacob van Zanten**, one of KLM's most senior and celebrated pilots, initiated the takeoff roll without an ATC takeoff clearance and over the objections (inadequately stated) of his first officer, Willem Schreuder.

The **authority gradient** is the CRM concept central to Tenerife: when the power differential between captain and junior crew is very steep, subordinate crew members fail to assertively communicate safety concerns. Van Zanten's legendary status created an extreme authority gradient. The first officer's concern was expressed obliquely ("Are we not clear, that Pan American?") rather than as an unambiguous challenge. A direct statement — "STOP, we do not have clearance" — might have prevented the accident. The **Dutch Aviation Safety Board** (Raad voor de Luchtvaart) report and the ALPA analysis of Tenerife became required reading in CRM training worldwide, and the accident is still used in every CRM course today.

**James Reason's Swiss-cheese model** (from *Human Error*, Cambridge University Press, **1990**) is the dominant conceptual framework for systemic accident analysis. Reason argues that complex systems have multiple layers of defenses — equipment, procedures, training, regulations, maintenance. Each layer has latent weaknesses or gaps (the "holes"). Under normal operations the holes rarely align. But when active failures (errors by operators) combine with latent conditions (management decisions, design flaws, inadequate procedures, organizational culture), the holes line up and an accident trajectory passes through all layers simultaneously. The model argues against blaming individuals and instead mandates investigation of **latent conditions** in the organization — a philosophy that underlies **SMS (Safety Management System)**, **ICAO Annex 19**, and the **"just culture"** concept.

The **SHELL model** (Software, Hardware, Environment, Liveware–Liveware) was developed by **Frank Hawkins** (1975) and popularized by **Elwyn Edwards** (1972). It depicts the human operator (central Liveware) at the interface of four domains:
- **S (Software)**: procedures, checklists, regulations, operating manuals.
- **H (Hardware)**: aircraft, cockpit design, instruments, automation.
- **E (Environment)**: physical environment (heat, vibration, noise), organizational environment.
- **L (Liveware)**: other humans — crew, controllers, maintenance.

Mismatches at any interface produce human error. The SHELL model is used in ICAO human factors training documents (**ICAO Doc 9683 — Human Factors Training Manual**) and in accident investigation to categorize contributing factors. The **NTSB** and **BEA (Bureau d'Enquêtes et d'Analyses, France)** use SHELL-derived frameworks in their final reports.

**Just culture** — articulated by **Sidney Dekker** in *Just Culture: Balancing Safety and Accountability* (**2007**) and operationalized by **Eurocontrol** — distinguishes between unacceptable behavior (willful violations, reckless conduct) and honest mistakes in the context of a complex system. A just culture does not punish honest errors, encouraging reporting; but it does hold individuals accountable for gross negligence or willful violations. The **FAA Aviation Safety Hotline** and the **ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System)** operated by **NASA** since **1975** are the US embodiments: pilots who voluntarily report safety incidents within 10 days and meet other criteria receive immunity from certificate action, generating an invaluable safety database of over 1.9 million de-identified reports.

slides.title: Automation dependency, AF447, spatial disorientation, and SMS
slides.body:
**Automation dependency** — the degradation of manual flying skills when flight crews over-rely on autopilot and FMS — became a headline safety concern in the 2000s. **Warren VanderBurgh**, an American Airlines check airman and aviation writer, coined the phrase **"children of the magenta line"** in a 1995 editorial in *Air Line Pilot* magazine, warning that a generation of pilots trained primarily on the **Boeing 757's** FMS magenta course line would lose the ability to hand-fly in degraded automation states. His concern proved prophetic. The **NTSB** safety study **SS-94/01** (Evaluation of Crew Resource Management and Line Operational Safety Audit Programs in the US Air Carrier Industry) documented increasing automation-related incidents. **FAA AC 120-111** (Upset Prevention and Recovery Training, **2015**) and **AC 120-109A** (Stall Prevention and Recovery Training, **2015**) now require manual flight proficiency training for Part 121 crews.

**Air France Flight 447** — an **Airbus A330-203** operating Paris Charles de Gaulle to Rio de Janeiro on June 1, **2009** — is the defining automation-dependency accident. At cruise altitude (FL350) over the mid-Atlantic, the aircraft's three **pitot tubes** (Thales BA model AA pitot probes, which had a known icing vulnerability in high-altitude tropical convective systems) iced over simultaneously, causing all three airspeed indications to become unreliable. The autopilot and autothrust disconnected, transferring control to the crew in **Alternate Law** — a reduced-protection flight control mode. Over the next 4 minutes and 24 seconds, the crew failed to recognize that the aircraft was in a **full aerodynamic stall** (nose high, very high angle of attack, falling at 10,000 ft/min) and made persistent nose-up inputs, deepening the stall. The aircraft struck the Atlantic Ocean, killing all **228 people** aboard.

The **BEA final report** (July **2012**) identified: (1) pitot probe icing causing unreliable airspeed; (2) upset of crew automation management when autopilot disconnected; (3) failure to recognize the stall despite aural stall warnings; (4) lack of manual flying practice at high altitude. The accident drove mandatory pitot probe replacement (Thales C16195AA probes on the A330/A340 fleet by **2011**, per **EASA AD 2009-0195**), mandatory upset recovery and high-altitude stall training, and ongoing debate about automation philosophy in **fly-by-wire** aircraft.

**Fly-by-wire (FBW)** — in which pilot control inputs are processed by flight control computers (**Airbus FCPC — Flight Control Primary Computers**, three redundant units on the A320 family) before being sent to control surfaces — enables **envelope protection**: the aircraft cannot be commanded outside safe speed/g/attitude limits in Normal Law. The **Airbus philosophy** ("hard limits") contrasts with the **Boeing philosophy** ("soft limits with pilot authority") on aircraft like the **777** and **787**. The AF447 accident renewed the debate: envelope protection was unavailable in Alternate Law, and the crew had no trained intuition for the aircraft's behavior without it.

**Spatial disorientation** — the inability to correctly perceive one's attitude, position, or motion relative to earth — kills approximately 15% of all fatal general aviation accidents each year (**FAA statistical data**). The vestibular system is deceived by sustained turns (the **leans**), by the **somatogravic illusion** (acceleration felt as pitch-up), and by the **graveyard spiral** (a progressive, unconscious roll into a tightening spiral perceived as level flight). **FAA FITS (FAA/Industry Training Standards)** and **AOPA's SkyAware** program train recognition and recovery. The famous **JFK Jr.** accident (July 16, **1999**, Piper Saratoga, Martha's Vineyard) is widely attributed to spatial disorientation in VFR-into-IMC conditions.

**Safety Management Systems (SMS)** — mandated by **ICAO Annex 19** (first edition **2013**, second edition **2016**) for air operators, airports, and ANSPs — provide a systematic, proactive approach to managing safety risk. An SMS has four components: safety policy; safety risk management (hazard identification + risk assessment); safety assurance (audits, performance monitoring); and safety promotion (training, culture). **FAA** implemented SMS requirements for Part 121 air carriers via rulemaking in **2024** (effective 2026). The SMS concept is built on Reason's Swiss-cheese model and Dekker's just-culture principles: organizations that report and analyze safety data before accidents occur drive down accident rates, as demonstrated by the **commercial aviation fatality rate drop from ~4 fatal accidents per million departures in 1970 to under 0.07 in 2023** (IATA data).

question.question: What was the primary human factors cause of the Tenerife disaster (1977) and which CRM concept does it most directly illustrate?
options: Crew fatigue; the KLM crew had exceeded duty time limits.

Authority gradient: KLM Captain van Zanten's exceptional seniority and prestige created a steep power differential that prevented First Officer Schreuder from assertively challenging the unauthorized takeoff. The term "authority gradient" describes the social distance between a dominant captain and subordinate crew members — when the gradient is too steep, junior crew suppress safety-critical communications or express concerns indirectly rather than as unambiguous stop commands. On Tenerife, the first officer's query ("Are we not clear, that Pan American?") was the only verbal challenge to van Zanten's decision to begin the takeoff roll without a clearance. It was not stated as a command to stop. The accident — which killed 583 people, still the largest death toll in aviation history — became the foundational case study for CRM training worldwide, demonstrating that technical skill in the captain is not sufficient if crew coordination fails. The Dutch and Spanish investigation reports, and the ALPA analysis, were distributed to airlines globally by 1979, directly informing the NASA workshop that created the term CRM.
Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT); the aircraft struck rising terrain in fog.
Spatial disorientation; the KLM captain lost attitude awareness in the fog.
question.explanation: Tenerife was an authority-gradient accident. Van Zanten's dominance suppressed assertive first-officer challenge. The Pan Am aircraft was still on the runway when KLM began its roll. Fog, ATC frequency congestion, and airport overcrowding were contributing factors, but the CRM lesson is authority gradient and assertive communication.

hints: Van Zanten was KLM's most celebrated captain and appeared in their advertising.
What did the first officer say — and not say — before the takeoff roll?
slides.workedSolution: The Tenerife disaster (March 27, 1977, Los Rodeos Airport, 583 fatalities) is the defining authority-gradient accident. Captain van Zanten's status and the first officer's failure to deliver an assertive stop command are the CRM failure. The accident drove the 1979 NASA CRM workshop and continues to define CRM training curricula.

question.question: Apply the Swiss-cheese model to Air France 447
question.goal: Using James Reason's Swiss-cheese model, identify the defensive layers that failed in Air France 447 (2009), the holes in each layer, and what latent conditions permitted the accident chain to run to completion.

steps.prompt: Layer 1 — Equipment: what was the hardware failure and what was the latent condition behind it?
steps.motivation: Identify the physical trigger and its organizational root.

acceptedAnswers: Thales BA pitot probes iced over; latent condition = known icing vulnerability not yet mandated for replacement

hints: The probes had a documented icing history in tropical convection.
steps.reveal: The Thales BA (model AA) pitot probes iced simultaneously in high-altitude tropical convective conditions. The latent condition: Airbus and the BEA had documented unreliable airspeed events from these probes on A330/A340 aircraft since 2002; Air France had issued a service bulletin recommending replacement with Thales C16195AA probes but had not yet replaced all aircraft. A mandatory AD (EASA AD 2009-0195) came only after AF447, not before — a classic latent organizational condition.

steps.prompt: Layer 2 — Automation design: what design hole allowed the crew to be surprised?
steps.motivation: The flight control mode change on autopilot disconnect.

acceptedAnswers: Autopilot disconnected and control laws degraded to Alternate Law, removing envelope protection; the crew was not adequately prepared for this state

hints: What happened to the flight control law when the autopilot disconnected?
steps.reveal: When all three pitot probes gave inconsistent readings, the autopilot and autothrust disconnected automatically, handing control to the crew. Control law simultaneously degraded from Normal Law (full envelope protection) to Alternate Law (reduced protection — no alpha floor, no high-speed protection). The crew had limited recent experience flying manually at cruise altitude in Alternate Law; the transition was abrupt and disorienting.

steps.prompt: Layer 3 — Training: what training hole contributed to the stall going unrecognized?
steps.motivation: Manual flying skills in degraded automation.

acceptedAnswers: Insufficient training in manual high-altitude flying and stall recognition/recovery without automation; crews rarely hand-flew at FL350

hints: How often did crews hand-fly at cruise altitude in 2009?
steps.reveal: In 2009, Air France (and most carriers) permitted and encouraged autopilot use from shortly after takeoff to shortly before landing. Crews rarely hand-flew at FL350. The BEA report found that pilot initial and recurrent training did not include manual flight at high altitude in degraded automation states. Stall characteristics at altitude (nose-high attitude, buffet, high angle of attack) were not reinforced. The stall warning sounded 75 times during the 4.5-minute descent; the crew did not recognize or correctly respond to it.

steps.prompt: Layer 4 — Procedures: what procedural hole existed for unreliable airspeed?
steps.motivation: Standard operating procedures as a defense layer.

acceptedAnswers: The unreliable airspeed procedure (set pitch attitude and thrust for cruise/descent) existed but was not executed; no immediate memory items were drilled to the point of automatic application

hints: What should a crew do when airspeed is unreliable?
steps.reveal: The Airbus FCOM unreliable airspeed procedure specifies: set pitch attitude (approximately 5° nose-up at cruise weight) and thrust (approximately 85% N1) and fly by attitude until speed can be cross-checked. This procedure was not initially executed. The BEA concluded it was not drilled as an immediate memory item and the crew did not recognize quickly enough that they were facing unreliable airspeed rather than some other malfunction.

question.question: The ASRS (Aviation Safety Reporting System) has received approximately 1,900,000 reports since its founding in 1975 through 2023 — a span of 48 years. What is the average number of reports submitted per year over that period? Round to the nearest hundred.

question.prompt: You are the captain of a Boeing 737-800 on approach to a rain-slicked runway. Your first officer has correctly identified that the approach is unstabilized (1,200 ft AGL, airspeed 20 knots above Vref, glide path not established). Your company's Stabilized Approach Policy requires a go-around below 500 ft if not stabilized, and recommends it at 1,000 ft. The first officer says: "Captain, we might want to think about a go-around." You are behind on checklists and feel pressure from the dispatcher about the tight turnaround. Using CRM concepts — authority gradient, assertive communication, TEM, and the stabilized approach policy — describe: (1) what the first officer should have said instead, (2) what the captain's correct response is, and (3) which human factors traps are active for each pilot. Reference at least two CRM or safety frameworks.

In 150 words or fewer, explain James Reason's Swiss-cheese model and state how it differs from blaming the individual who made the final error. Then name one accident covered in this lesson and identify two specific 'holes' in two different defensive layers that aligned to produce that accident.
question.rubric: Should correctly describe the Swiss-cheese model: multiple defensive layers each with latent weaknesses; accidents occur when holes align and an accident trajectory passes through all layers simultaneously. Must contrast this with individual blame: the model argues the operator at the sharp end is the inheritor of upstream latent conditions, not the root cause. Should name one accident: Tenerife (1977, authority gradient hole in crew training/culture layer + ATC procedures hole in radio procedures layer + fog/congestion in environmental layer) OR Air France 447 (2009, pitot probe design/maintenance hole + training hole for high-altitude manual flight + procedural hole for unreliable airspeed). Should cite Reason's Human Error (1990) or James Reason by name. Bonus for mentioning just culture (Dekker) or ICAO SMS (Annex 19) as practical applications of the Swiss-cheese philosophy.
